title: Feed-Forward Loops and Network Motifs
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter is assembled from two pieces of material that, unusually, do not come from the same lecture: a 2004 slide deck on the excitation-and-adaptation model of bacterial chemotaxis, and a 2014 lecture recording on network motifs and feed-forward loops. Rather than force a connection the sources do not make, the chapter treats them as two independent parts. Part I assumes the receptor/methylation picture of chemotaxis signalling from earlier lectures. Part II assumes only the idea of a directed gene-regulation network — who regulates whom — and the notion of a network motif (a subgraph pattern that recurs far more often than chance), which the course had already introduced through auto-regulation. ## Part I — Excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis The model is Spiro, Parkinson and Othmer's "A model of excitation and adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis" (*PNAS* **94**, 7263–7268, 1997), built around the Tar–CheA–CheW complex: Tar is the aspartate receptor, CheW couples it to CheA, the kinase that autophosphorylates and then passes its phosphate on to the response regulators CheY and CheB. ### The model's assumptions To keep the model tractable, it makes eight simplifications: 1. Tar is the only receptor type considered, and CheW and CheA are always bound to it. 2. The receptor's methylation sites are methylated in a fixed order, not at random. 3. Only the three highest methylation states are tracked. 4. Only phosphorylated CheB (CheB-P) demethylates the receptor. 5. Phosphorylation of CheA does not affect ligand binding or unbinding. 6. CheR (the methyltransferase) binding to Tar does not affect ligand (un)binding or CheA phosphorylation. 7. CheZ, the phosphatase that removes phosphate from CheY-P, is not itself regulated. 8. Phosphotransfer from the complex to CheY or to CheB does not depend on the receptor's ligand occupancy or methylation state. Two further facts about the rates matter for what follows: ligand-bound receptor states autophosphorylate more slowly than unbound ones, and CheR methylates ligand-bound states faster than unbound ones. Both push in the same direction — occupying the receptor with ligand lowers the phosphorylation rate and raises the methylation rate — and that opposition is what produces adaptation. The model separates cleanly into three timescales: ligand binding and unbinding are fast, methylation and demethylation are slow, and phosphorylation/dephosphorylation sit in between. ### The response to a step in ligand Consider stepping the aspartate concentration up and following the complex through the three timescales in turn. - **~1 ms.** Ligand binds essentially instantly; the fraction of ligand-bound complex rises at once. - **~5 s.** Because ligand-bound complexes autophosphorylate poorly, the total pool of phosphorylated complex — CheA-P — falls gradually as the existing phosphorylated pool turns over. CheB-P falls with it (assumption 8: the same complex phosphorylates both CheY and CheB). Low CheA-P means low CheY-P, and since CheY-P is what drives tumbling, tumbling is suppressed. - **~50 s.** With CheB-P low, demethylation — which only CheB-P can do — is effectively switched off, while CheR keeps methylating (faster, in fact, on the ligand-bound states). The receptor's methylation level climbs slowly. CheA-P and CheY-P are still low, so tumbling is still suppressed. - **Beyond that.** Higher methylation states autophosphorylate more readily, so as methylation climbs, CheA-P — and with it CheY-P — slowly climbs back to its original, pre-stimulus level. Tumbling resumes at the original rate. ### Why this counts as "perfect" adaptation The slide deck's own title for this model is "fine-tuned model for perfect adaptation." The point of the mechanism above is that CheA-P — and hence CheY-P, and hence tumbling frequency — returns to its *original* level, not merely to some new lower level, regardless of the size of the ligand step. The cell's behaviour ends up depending on whether the ligand concentration is currently rising or falling, not on its absolute value, because the receptor's slow methylation state is what re-centres the fast response. The deck also points to Barkai and Leibler, "Robustness in simple biochemical networks" (*Nature* **387**, 913–917, 1997), for a complementary argument about how robust this adaptation is to the cell's enzyme concentrations — but the figures for that part were not preserved in the source conversion, so that argument is not reproduced here. ## Part II — Network motifs and the feed-forward loop ### Is a subgraph a coincidence? A network motif is a subgraph pattern that occurs in a real network far more often than it would in a comparable random network. Auto-regulation (a node regulating itself: one node, one edge) was established earlier in the course as one such motif. The question now is how to make "far more often than chance" precise, and what other patterns pass the test — in particular, the **feed-forward loop**: $X$ regulates $Y$, and both $X$ and $Y$ regulate $Z$. As a subgraph this has $n = 3$ nodes and $g = 3$ edges. Take the *E. coli* transcription network used in the course: roughly $N \approx 400$ genes/proteins as nodes and $E \approx 500$ regulatory edges. Two summary numbers matter: - **Sparseness**, $p = E / N^2$: the fraction of all $N^2$ possible directed edges that actually appear. Here $p \ll 1$ — a typical pair of genes is not connected. - **Mean degree**, $\lambda = E/N$: the average number of outgoing (equivalently, incoming) edges per node. Here $\lambda$ is just over 1. $\lambda$ being close to 1 hides something the average alone does not show: the out-degree distribution is heavy-tailed. Most proteins have *no* outgoing regulatory edges at all — because most proteins are not transcription factors, so they cannot directly affect anyone else's transcription — while a handful of transcription factors regulate many genes. The average is real, but it is not typical of any single node. ### Expected count of a subgraph in a random network Model the null network as Erdős–Rényi: $N$ nodes, each of the $N^2$ possible directed edges present independently with probability $p$. To count how many copies of a given $n$-node, $g$-edge subgraph pattern to expect: choose the $n$ nodes to play the pattern's roles ($\approx N^n$ ways, for $N$ much larger than $n$), divide by $a$, the symmetry factor — the number of ways of relabelling the pattern's nodes that give back the same set of edges (for the feed-forward loop $X,Y,Z$ play distinguishable roles, so $a=1$; for a 3-cycle $X\to Y\to Z\to X$, the three cyclic rotations all give the same pattern, so $a=3$) — and multiply by the probability $p^g$ that all $g$ required edges are present: $$\langle \#\text{subgraph}\rangle \approx \frac{N^{\,n}}{a}\,p^{\,g}.$$ Substituting $p = \lambda/N$ turns this into something more useful: $$\langle \#\text{subgraph}\rangle \approx \frac{\lambda^{\,g}}{a}\,N^{\,n-g}.$$ Whenever $n = g$ — as for auto-regulation and for the feed-forward loop — the $N$ dependence vanishes: the expected count does not grow with the size of the network, only with $\lambda$. Since $\lambda \approx 1$ in gene-regulation networks of very different sizes, this expected count is of order 1 regardless of whether the network has 500 nodes or 5,000. That is what makes "a handful expected, dozens observed" a meaningful test for a network motif independent of network size. ### The feed-forward loop in *E. coli*, and a better null model Applying this: the *E. coli* network was observed to contain **42** feed-forward loops. Because each triple of nodes is an approximately independent rare event, the count over many random networks with the same $N$ and $p$ should be roughly Poisson-distributed; simulating the Erdős–Rényi null directly gives an expectation of **1.7 ± 1.3**. Forty-two against fewer than two is strong evidence that the feed-forward loop is a network motif, not a coincidence. But is Erdős–Rényi the right null model? It only matches the network's *mean* degree, not its actual, heavy-tailed *degree distribution*. A stricter null model is **degree-preserving randomisation**: repeatedly pick two edges at random and swap their endpoints, many times, so that every node keeps its exact in- and out-degree while the network is otherwise randomised. Against this null model, the expected count is **7 ± 5** — noticeably higher than the Erdős–Rényi estimate, though still well below 42. The gap between 1.7 and 7 has a mechanistic explanation, and it is worth being careful about it, because — as the lecture points out — a purely verbal argument here is easy to get backwards. What matters is specifically *out*-degree, not in-degree: a real transcription factor $X$ with many outgoing edges creates many opportunities for one of its targets $Y$ to also regulate another target $Z$, completing a feed-forward loop. A degree-preserving randomisation keeps that fan-out exactly as concentrated as it is in the real network, whereas an Erdős–Rényi network spreads edges out roughly evenly and so under-produces exactly this configuration. The typical target node $Z$, by contrast, is not unusual under either null model — the in-degree distribution is closer to Erdős–Rényi-like to begin with — so the extra feed-forward loops come from the hubs on the regulating side, not from anything special about the regulated side. Milo et al., "Network Motifs: Simple Building Blocks of Complex Networks" (*Science*, 2002), extended this analysis (against a degree-preserving null) beyond *E. coli* to yeast, to the *C. elegans* neuronal connectome, to food webs, to logic-chip designs, and to the World Wide Web. Feed-forward loops were overrepresented in the gene-regulation and neuronal networks but not in food webs, where other patterns were the motifs instead — the lesson being that which subgraphs recur depends on the constraints and function specific to each kind of network, not on some universal property of networks in general. ### The coherent type-1 loop: a sign-sensitive delay Now fix signs: **coherent type-1** means $X$ activates $Y$, and both $X$ and $Y$ activate $Z$, with the two inputs to $Z$ combined by some logic gate. Take the gate to be AND first. $X$ has its own input signal $S_x$ and $Y$ has its own signal $S_y$; assume $X$ itself is always present, so that $S_x$ switches $X$ into its active form $X^*$ essentially instantly — this is just a small molecule binding, fast compared to any change in protein concentration. $Y^*$, by contrast, has to be made or lost by ordinary transcription and translation, on the slow, generation-time scale. Suppose $S_y$ is present throughout and $S_x$ is switched on and then off. Turning $S_x$ on: $X^*$ appears immediately, but $Z$ needs *both* $X^*$ and $Y^*$ above threshold (AND gate), and $Y^*$ only climbs gradually — so $Z$'s rise is delayed relative to $X^*$'s. Turning $S_x$ off: $X^*$ disappears immediately, and because it is an AND gate, that alone is enough to shut $Z$ off at once — even though $Y^*$ is still present and only beginning its own, unhurried decay. So there is a delay on activation but none on deactivation: a **sign-sensitive delay**, present when turning the downstream gene on but not when turning it off, compared with $X$ regulating $Z$ directly with no intermediate step. Two variations make the argument's dependence on the gate explicit. Swap AND for OR: since either input alone now suffices, $Z$ tracks the fast $X^*$ directly in both directions, and the delay disappears — the circuit collapses onto simple regulation. Fix $S_x = 1$ (so $X$'s contribution to the AND gate is already satisfied) and instead switch $S_y$: with the AND condition on $X^*$ permanently met, $Z$'s response is governed entirely by $Y^*$, again with no delay in either direction. The delay is specifically a property of *which* input changes and *which* gate combines them, not a generic feature of having two upstream regulators. Experimentally, this is checked by putting $X$ and $Y$ each on independent inducible promoters, decoupling them from their natural regulation, and reading out $Z$ (e.g. as a fluorescent reporter) as a function of the two inputs directly — mapping out the truth table rather than inferring it. ### The incoherent type-1 loop: a pulse generator The other feed-forward loop found to be overrepresented (about half of the observed loops in *E. coli* and yeast are one type or the other) is **incoherent type-1**: $X$ activates $Y$, $X$ activates $Z$, but $Y$ *represses* $Z$ — the two paths to $Z$ disagree in sign. With $S_y$ already present when $S_x$ switches on: $Z$ starts rising immediately (same as before, since $Y^*$ starts low), but as $Y^*$ accumulates it crosses its own threshold and begins repressing $Z$, pulling it back down. The result is a transient pulse rather than a step. How far $Z$ falls back down depends on how complete the repression is. With strong, complete repression, this is a **pulse generator**: $Z$ turns on and then off again even while $S_x$ stays on. With incomplete repression, $Z$ overshoots and settles at a lower steady level — which, compared to plain regulation, gets $Z$ up to a useful level *faster*. Made precise: define $t_{on}$ as the time to reach half of the eventual steady-state concentration, $Z_{eq}/2$. Under simple regulation, $Z$ approaches $Z_{eq}$ by ordinary exponential growth, with $t_{on,\text{simple}}$ set by the generation/protein-lifetime timescale. Under the incoherent type-1 loop with partial repression, the overshoot crosses $Z_{eq}/2$ much sooner than that plain exponential would, so $t_{on} \ll t_{on,\text{simple}}$. That reframes a question the course had already asked in a different context — what speeds up a transcriptional response — as a menu of three mechanisms: | Strategy | Effect | |---|---| | Decrease protein lifetime (more degradation) | Decreases both $t_{on}$ and $t_{off}$ | | Negative auto-regulation | Decreases $t_{on}$ only | | Incoherent type-1 feed-forward loop (partial repression) | Decreases $t_{on}$ only | Negative auto-regulation makes a burst of protein and then clamps itself at a new, lower steady level once the repression threshold is crossed — that clamps the rise, but turning the gene off entirely still leaves the protein decaying at its ordinary lifetime, so $t_{off}$ is untouched. The incoherent loop speeds $t_{on}$ the same way, through an overshoot rather than a clamp, and for the same reason leaves $t_{off}$ alone. The general point behind both: there are many more ways to make a protein quickly than to get rid of it quickly, because turning it off is bounded below by ordinary decay and dilution, which no amount of circuit design gets around, while turning it on can be actively engineered. ### Why transcription networks are slow, and what that implies All of the timescales above are set by the generation time or the protein lifetime — minutes to hours. That is intrinsically too slow for everything a cell needs to do: transcription and translation both take time, and beyond that, changing a *concentration* of protein is slow by nature. For faster responses, cells instead build networks that change a protein's *state* rather than its concentration — phosphorylation being the standard example, exactly the mechanism used above to let $S_x$ switch $X$ into $X^*$ essentially instantly. Protein-only networks (for instance MAPK cascades, which this course does not cover but which follow the same logic) can perform information processing much faster than any transcriptional circuit, because no new synthesis or degradation is required. ### Temporal programs: ordering a pathway's enzymes Extending feed-forward-loop-style reasoning to larger structures gives temporal programs — this follows chapter 5 of the course's textbook, which is not itself reproduced here. Consider a metabolic or biosynthetic pathway, a chain of enzymes $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots$ each converting one metabolite into the next. When a new carbon source appears, or a product is newly needed, making $Z_2$ before $Z_1$ exists wastes energy — there is nothing yet for $Z_2$ to act on. The cell would rather make $Z_1$ first, then $Z_2$, and so on, in pathway order. A **single-input module (SIM)** does this with one transcription factor $X$ (often auto-regulating, to stabilise its own level) activating every $Z_i$ directly. Note that "$X$ activates many targets" is not by itself a network motif — a degree-preserving null model already expects some nodes to have many outgoing edges, since the degree distribution is heavy-tailed anyway. What makes a SIM a genuine motif is the further, non-generic fact that these particular $Z_i$ are regulated *only* by $X$, more often than chance predicts. The ordering mechanism: give each $Z_i$ a different activation threshold $K_i$ for the same rising signal $X(t)$, which climbs continuously from zero once $X$ is switched on. If $K_1 < K_2 < \cdots < K_n$, the genes switch on in exactly that order as $X(t)$ climbs past each threshold in turn. An alternative design — a cascade, $Z_1$ itself required to activate $Z_2$, and so on — also gives sequential order, but each step costs a full generation-time delay. That is appropriate on developmental timescales spanning many generations, but far too slow if what is wanted is a few minutes between successive genes; the SIM-with-thresholds design gets that instead, at the cost of only about one generation of usable dynamic range from the first threshold to the last. ### Turning the pathway off: LIFO, FIFO, and the multi-output feed-forward loop A first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue empties in the order it filled (a checkout line); a last-in-first-out (LIFO) queue empties in the reverse order (a pile of papers, where the most recent arrival is dealt with first and the oldest may never be reached). In the plain single-input module, the *same* thresholds $K_1 < \cdots < K_n$ govern both directions of the same monotonic $X(t)$: as $X(t)$ falls again, it drops back below $K_n$ first and $K_1$ last, so the genes switch off in the reverse of the order they switched on — $Z_n$ first, $Z_1$ last. That is a LIFO queue, and it is the wrong one here: switching off $Z_n$ first leaves the enzymes below it in the chain still active, so the metabolite it was consuming piles up. What is wanted instead is FIFO: switch off $Z_1$ first, stopping material entering the pathway, and only then shut down the rest in the same order, draining the pipeline cleanly. A **multi-output feed-forward loop** gets FIFO. Structure: $X$ activates $Y$; both $X$ and $Y$ activate every $Z_i$, combined this time by an OR gate. $X$'s thresholds for the $Z_i$ are $K_1, \ldots, K_n$; $Y$'s thresholds for the same genes are a *separate* set, $K_1', \ldots, K_n'$; and $Y$ itself is switched on by $X$ with its own threshold $K_y$, so $Y$'s rise lags behind $X$'s. At onset, $Y$ has not yet caught up, so it is the $K_i$ thresholds — on the fast, $X$-driven input — that decide the turn-on order, exactly as in the plain SIM. At shutoff, by contrast, it is $Y$ and its own thresholds $K_i'$ that are doing the (OR-gated) work, because $Y$'s slower dynamics are what are still active during the decay. Choosing the $K_i'$ in the *reverse* order of the $K_i$ — the gene with the smallest $K_i$ given the largest $K_i'$, and so on — makes the shutoff order match the turn-on order: FIFO. This is not hypothetical: the flagellar biosynthesis pathway in *E. coli* and other bacteria is observed to switch its component genes on in assembly order and off again in that *same* order — a FIFO queue, implemented (on this account) by a multi-output feed-forward loop of exactly this kind. ## Sources **Part I** is drawn entirely from `computational-biology/mit-ocw/8591j/2004/lectures/08-notes.md` — the 2004 MIT OCW 8.591J lecture-8 slide deck. That deck is a machine reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer (route: `llm`, fidelity: `reconstructed`), and it covers only the Spiro–Parkinson–Othmer (1997) chemotaxis excitation-and-adaptation model; the model's assumptions, the fast/slow/intermediate timescale labelling, and the step-response walk-through (~1 ms, ~5 s, ~50 s) are all as given there. The deck's reference to Barkai and Leibler (1997) on robustness is named but not reproduced: its figures were removed from the source for copyright reasons and are not available in this conversion. **Part II** is drawn entirely from `computational-biology/mit-ocw/8591j/2014/recordings/recordings/zjtvmkge8-8.md`, a captioned 2014 MIT OCW 8.591J lecture recording. Roughly: network structure and sparseness, [00:00]–[07:47]; counting subgraphs and the Erdős–Rényi expected-count formula, [07:47]–[17:26]; the observed feed-forward-loop count and the degree-preserving null model, [17:26]–[27:21]; Milo et al. (2002) and the range of networks it covers, [27:21]–[29:34]; the coherent type-1 loop, AND vs OR gates, and the sign-sensitive delay, [29:34]–[44:08]; the incoherent type-1 loop, the pulse generator, and the three speed-up strategies, [44:08]–[58:36]; why transcription is slow, [56:21]–[58:36]; single-input modules and threshold ordering, [58:36]–[1:07:23]; FIFO vs LIFO and the multi-output feed-forward loop, [1:07:23]–[1:21:02]. The lecture refers throughout to "the chapter you just read" and to "Uri's book" — the course's systems-biology textbook (chapters 4 and 5 in particular) — and to Milo, R. et al., "Network Motifs: Simple Building Blocks of Complex Networks," *Science* (2002); neither the textbook chapters nor the paper itself are part of the supplied material, and their content beyond what the lecture states directly is not reproduced here. **The mismatch.** These two files were supplied together for this chapter slot, but they are not from the same lecture: the slide deck is 2004 lecture 8 on bacterial chemotaxis, and the transcript is an unrelated 2014 recording on network motifs. No connection between the two is asserted or implied anywhere above.
